lessons.title: How Loudness Became a Virtue
lessons.key_idea: In the early twentieth century, Western culture shifted from valuing inner character to prizing outgoing personality, creating an Extrovert Ideal that still shapes how we judge people.

lessons.title: Why Solitude Sparks Creativity
lessons.key_idea: Constant teamwork and group brainstorming often produce worse ideas than focused time alone, as shown by Steve Wozniak building the first Apple computer working by himself.

lessons.title: Born Sensitive: The Science of Temperament
lessons.key_idea: Jerome Kagan's research found that babies who react strongly to new stimulation often grow into cautious, introverted adults, showing that temperament is partly inborn.

lessons.title: Stretching Beyond Your Nature
lessons.key_idea: Introverts can act like extroverts for work or causes they care about, as professor Brian Little does when lecturing, but they need restorative niches to recharge afterward.

lessons.title: Why Extroverts Chase the Prize
lessons.key_idea: Extroverts tend to be more driven by the thrill of reward, while introverts pause to weigh risks, a caution that can protect groups from reckless decisions.

lessons.title: The Surprising Strength of Soft Power
lessons.key_idea: Quiet persistence and gentle conviction can change the world, as Rosa Parks showed when her calm refusal sparked a movement.

lessons.title: Building a World for Both
lessons.key_idea: Homes, schools, workplaces and relationships thrive when introverts and extroverts understand each other's needs and make room for both quiet and bold strengths.

plan.title: Quiet
plan.author: Susan Cain
plan.confidence_note: I know this book's main arguments, structure and key examples well, though I'd avoid quoting precise figures or wording from memory.
plan.one_liner: Our culture rewards the loudest voice, but the quiet ones may hold the most power.
plan.summary: Susan Cain argues that modern Western culture, especially in America, has built itself around an Extrovert Ideal. This is the belief that the best person is bold, sociable and comfortable in the spotlight. She traces how this ideal grew, and how it shapes our schools, offices and even our ideas about good leadership. Drawing on psychology and neuroscience, she shows that introversion is a real temperament, partly inborn, linked to how sensitive we are to stimulation. Far from being a flaw, it brings strengths like deep focus, careful thinking, persistence and quiet influence. Cain explores how introverts can stretch beyond their nature when something matters to them, and why they need time to recharge. She ends with practical advice for workplaces, relationships and parents raising quiet children, making the case for a world that values both styles.
